title: Fable is Back: Here's What You Should Try First
dek: Two threads today: the industry's frantic hunt for cheaper inference — from OpenAI's secret 50% trick to Base44's own model — and the return of Fable 5 after 19 days offline. NLW closes with a practical guide to what you should actually try Fable on first.

oneIdea.headline: Fable 5 is back — but the real story is what you do with it in the one free week.
oneIdea.summary: After 19 days offline, Anthropic's Fable 5 returns for all global users, with 50% of weekly usage subsidized until July 7th. The conventional wisdom says save it for your hardest technical problems. NLW pushes back: from first-hand use, Fable is dramatically better at strategic thinking (it holds its ground under pushback instead of caving) and at rubric-driven writing (fewer AI-isms, better instruction following). Meanwhile the entire industry is racing to cut inference costs — the connective tissue behind OpenAI's secret technique, Base44's own model, and the shift toward open-weight deployment.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Cheaper inference could quietly cut the running cost of your AI scribe
items.body: The edition's lead is that inference costs are dropping fast — OpenAI claims a 50 percent efficiency gain, and several founders reported cutting their AI spend by more than 75 percent in a day with no loss of quality. If NLW is right that this is real engineering progress, the ambient scribes and letter-drafting tools a surgery already uses should get cheaper or more capable at the same price over the next year. If Zitron is right that the labs are simply subsidising tokens they still lose money on, today's low prices are a customer-acquisition loss-leader that can be withdrawn — so a practice should treat a very cheap AI vendor as a flight risk, not a permanent saving, and keep the contract terms and an exit plan in view.

items.title: 'Fall back to a smaller model' is now a clinical-safety question, not just a billing one
items.body: A recurring theme is models being quietly downgraded for routine or low-engagement use — OpenAI testing its cheaper technique on its least-active users, and Anthropic's note that some routine tasks 'fall back' to a smaller model. For a scribe summarising a consultation, the practical question is whether you can tell which model actually produced a given note, and whether quality is being silently traded for cost. When procuring, ask the vendor to state which model transcribes and summarises, whether that can change without notice, and how the tool flags low-confidence output — because a summary that drops a red-flag symptom is a safety issue regardless of who is subsidising the compute.

items.title: Own-model and open-weight trend may favour on-premise NHS deployment
items.body: Base44 built its own fine-tuned model to control cost and latency, and AWS noted enterprises shifting toward open-weight models. If that trend holds, it strengthens the case that clinically sensitive tools could eventually run on models hosted within NHS or UK data boundaries rather than sending consultation audio to a US frontier lab — relevant for information-governance and DPIA discussions at PCN level, though nothing here changes the current position that most scribes still call an external frontier model.

the_other_side.text: NLW reads the wave of inference cost cuts — OpenAI's undisclosed 50 percent trick, founders reporting 75 percent savings overnight, Base44 rolling its own model — as the industry engineering its way out of the compute crunch, a bullish sign. Zitron argues the exact opposite: nobody has ever shown the labs are actually profitable on inference, and cheaper tokens do not fix that. He notes Anthropic's own March affidavit implies it spent roughly three dollars of compute for every dollar of revenue, that Coatue found 85 percent of its 2025 revenue was API calls yet it still loses money, and that subscriptions let users "burn between $8 and $13.50 of every dollar." His conclusion: "If the margins were good, they'd be sharing the margins." Falling inference costs, to him, are a race to subsidise demand, not a path to sustainability.

the_truth_beneath.text: Both men orbit one variable: whether the cost of running these models can fall to genuinely unsubsidised profitability, or whether cheaper inference is just subsidy in a new suit. Both accept that token prices are collapsing fast and that the leading labs still post enormous losses. The empirical question is whether falling unit costs actually reach positive gross margin on real, paid usage; the observable that settles it is an audited inference margin — cost per token served against price charged — disclosed rather than asserted. The residue is worldview: NLW reads a 50 percent efficiency trick as engineering escaping the crunch, Zitron reads the same figure as proof they must keep cutting because the economics never worked. NLW is vindicated if a lab publishes real inference profit; Zitron if capex and compute deals keep outrunning it. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain with a paid newsletter — and the signal is where they agree: prices are falling. Watch whether any lab discloses an audited inference margin rather than a run rate.

headlines.headline: OpenAI cut inference costs in half — sort of
headlines.summary: The Information reports OpenAI found an optimization technique that halved inference requirements for existing models, letting it serve all signed-out ChatGPT users on just 100 GPUs. The technique wasn't disclosed; speculation ranges from quantization to query routing — and none of those improve larger models without quality trade-offs.

headlines.headline: There's still no free lunch on inference
headlines.summary: NLW's caution: this is likely a smaller breakthrough than the headline suggests, and it's being tested on OpenAI's least-engaged users — which could be a reasonable first step or a hint of quality-degradation risk. Don't treat it as a silver bullet for the compute crunch.

headlines.headline: This is a very important secret sauce for them that they don't even want to tell other OpenAI employees about.
headlines.summary: The Information's Stefanie Palazzolo argues OpenAI is holding the technique close because if it leaked, rival labs could quickly adopt it to lower their own costs.

headlines.headline: There's nothing my mom actually asks of her AI products that needs to be done by the frontier.
headlines.summary: Benchmark Ventures' Everett Randall's "AI mom test" captures why quality reductions may be tolerable for casual users — likely the exact segment OpenAI's new technique targets.

headlines.headline: Five founders cut inference spend 75%+ with little effort, no performance change, better latency.
headlines.summary: 20 Minute VC's Harry Stebbings said founders from 10-person startups to a $200 billion public company all reported major inference savings in 24 hours: "The times they are a-changing."

headlines.headline: Base44 builds its own model to control costs
headlines.summary: Vibe coding platform Base44 launched Base1, fine-tuning an open-source base model on hundreds of millions of user interactions — the same playbook as Cursor's Composer. The bet: a model that only needs to be good at building web apps can rival the frontier while giving Base44 control over cost, latency, and quality.

headlines.headline: Owning more of that intelligence becomes just as important as owning the infrastructure around it.
headlines.summary: Base44's Shlomo frames the strategic logic: as AI becomes central to how software is created, controlling the model itself — paired with the harness — is a core moat.

headlines.headline: AWS drops $1B on forward-deployed engineers
headlines.summary: AWS is investing a billion dollars in a new unit of forward-deployed engineers to help customers set up AI tools, joining OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft in the FTE race. It's upskilling salespeople into "solution architects" and focusing on healthcare, government, and financial services.

headlines.headline: Open weight models are definitely gaining traction — price performance, but also they service the task.
headlines.attribution: Vasquez, AWS Frontier AI Engineering and Services
headlines.summary: AWS's Vasquez noted the big enterprise shift toward AI budget optimization rather than just capability deployment, with open-source and open-weight models gaining ground.

headlines.headline: Claude Tag is coming to Microsoft Teams
headlines.summary: Anthropic told Microsoft it plans to bring Claude Tag to Teams. It's an organization-centric agent — not tied to any user — with persistent memory and tool access, and it actually calls the full Claude Code suite rather than plain Claude.

headlines.headline: The most exciting things in AI are plug-ins in Word or Excel... we have a structural position in knowledge work.
headlines.summary: Satya Nadella framed third-party agents like Claude as reinforcing Microsoft's ecosystem — though NLW wonders whether the tune changes as Claude gets more endemic across knowledge work.

headlines.headline: SpaceX offers half-price Starlink to quell Memphis backlash
headlines.summary: To ease controversy over its Colossus data centers — powered off-grid by 46 gas turbines running without a permit — SpaceX is offering greater-Memphis residents half-price Starlink and free hardware, and recommitted to a wastewater treatment plant. The US government recently intervened to shut down the turbines, calling Colossus a national security matter.

headlines.headline: Applaud the direction, but go a lot harder than half-price
headlines.summary: NLW is glad data center operators are starting to cut communities into the benefits — but says making residents become customers to get a discount is far too small a gesture. Still, encouraging signs that these relationships are being rethought.

headlines.headline: Fable 5 is officially back after 19 days
headlines.summary: Anthropic announced the Department of Commerce lifted export controls, restoring Fable 5 for all global paid subscribers starting July 1st. A short subsidy extension covers up to 50% of weekly usage limits until July 7th; after that, access requires purchasing usage credits.

headlines.headline: Anthropic: the jailbreak exposed no unique dangerous capability
headlines.summary: Anthropic said testing confirmed many less-capable models — including GPT-5.5 and Kimi K2.7 — could identify the same vulnerabilities Fable 5 flagged, and the reported technique only involved routine defensive cybersecurity work. It trained a new classifier claiming a 99% block rate, validated by Commerce's Center for AI Standards and Innovation as "extraordinarily strong."

headlines.headline: This opacity will not lend itself well to a stable, investable, trustworthy industry over time.
headlines.summary: Policy advisor Dean Ball welcomed Fable's return but noted no one knows what Anthropic actually did to make the model safe or how it applies to other models in the licensing queue. Still, he called a two-week review timeline "not insane" and real progress.

headlines.headline: The first rule of Fable Club is you do not ask too many questions.
headlines.summary: Miles Brundage captured the prevailing policy mood: even with lots of open questions about what exactly Anthropic agreed to, people are cautiously optimistic just to have the model back.

headlines.headline: We're living with a framework that requires heavy judgment
headlines.summary: NLW's read: there's a semblance of a practical framework now, but a lot of subjectivity goes into assessing risks. The best-case outcome is an efficient process with faster review for incremental updates — a bad outcome would be every capable release triggering the same weeks-long review and slowing the pace of breakthroughs.

headlines.headline: Only a small fraction of coding tasks fall back to Opus
headlines.summary: The announcement's line that "some routine tasks like coding and debugging will fall back to Opus 4.8" sparked backlash that the relaunch was "fake." The Claude Code team clarified the wording was loose: only a small fraction of routine coding and debugging tasks get flagged and reverted to Opus.

headlines.headline: Anthropic ships Claude Sonnet 5 — its most agentic Sonnet
headlines.summary: Pitched as nearly as good as Opus 4.8 for a fraction of the cost, Sonnet 5 sits a few points shy of Opus on major coding benchmarks but posted a big jump on GDPVal, hinting at strong end-to-end agentic follow-through. NLW suspects the timing means Anthropic didn't expect Fable 5 back so soon.

headlines.headline: Sonnet 5 can cost more than Opus — even more than Fable
headlines.summary: Artificial Analysis found Sonnet 5 used ~40% more output tokens and ~3x the agentic turns of Sonnet 4.6; on the full benchmark it was more expensive than Opus 4.8 and even Fable. Without promotional pricing, it costs more per task than Opus — leaving many asking what it's actually for.

headlines.headline: You have to use it wildly differently... it's basically an automatic Ralph loop.
headlines.summary: Ben Davis argued Sonnet 5 is good but inefficient and slow — spawning sub-agents, stacking PRs, reviewing itself adversarially. Others suggest the real framing is Fable 5 as the intelligent advisor and Sonnet 5 as the fast implementer running the sub-agents.

headlines.headline: Fable 5 blows the field away on strategic thinking
headlines.summary: NLW's first-hand experience: unlike GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8, which cave immediately under pushback and over-interpret instructions, Fable 5 accepts part of a critique while holding its ground on other parts — behavior he's never seen from another model. And it doesn't burn many tokens, so it won't chew through the 50% usage limit.

headlines.headline: Fable is far better at rubric-driven writing
headlines.summary: Contrary to Every's vibe check, NLW found Fable 5 much better at instruction-following, with fewer AI-isms and less try-hard prose. His suspicion: when you have a clear rubric or examples of good writing, Fable meets that standard far better than prior models — even if it's not necessarily better at blank-page writing.

headlines.headline: A one-week playbook for using Fable without going bankrupt
headlines.summary: Panjwani's advice: use Fable 5 for planning not implementation (delegate coding to GPT-5.5 via Codex), ask it for improvements on your most valuable projects, use other models to surface your hardest problems then have Fable propose solutions, and review Fable's output with GPT Pro. NLW agrees on the hard technical problems half but pushes hard on also using it for strategy and writing.
